fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd approach it the same way I approach everything, which is to look at the cause-effect relationships that have played out over and over again through history, and then diversify, because I don't know for sure how it's going to go.

So the first thing is, I'd look at the fundamentals. Is the place earning more than it's spending? Does it have a good balance sheet, so it's not drowning in debt? Those are the basics, like a doctor looking at a patient's vital signs. Then I'd look at whether the people are civil with each other. Is there internal order, or is there the kind of polarization where the left and the right can't agree on anything and you're at risk of some form of civil conflict? History shows that when you have large wealth gaps and large values gaps at the same time, and then a bad economic period, you get disorder, and that's a very bad place to have your money and your business. Then, is the country at risk of international conflict? I'd much rather be in a neutral country during a period of great power conflict than in one of the countries doing the fighting. And then, is it investing in education, in innovation, in productivity? Because that's what produces the prosperity over time.

We actually measure these things. We have 18 or so measures that we apply to 24 of the leading countries, and we rate them. And what you see is that the countries that are financially sound, that are internally orderly, that are not going to be in a war, and that have a good education system tend to be the good places. Singapore is a good example. Switzerland. The UAE, in a way. Some of the countries in Southeast Asia, Indonesia, Vietnam. India has a lot of potential if it can get through its reforms.

But the most important thing is, don't bet on one. I've been doing this for over fifty years, and the biggest lesson is that I can be wrong, and the world changes. So I'd build the business so that it has roots in a few places, it's not dependent on any one government's goodwill, and it can shift if the circumstances shift. That's just diversification, and diversification is the one thing in investing that reduces your risk without reducing your expected return. The same principle applies to where you build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses education, innovation, and productivity as drivers of prosperity, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends building the business with roots in a few places and avoiding dependence on any one country.

r003.rationale: It says the world and circumstances change, so a business should be able to shift locations rather than rely on one place.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing is to recognize that you don't have to pick one country, and in today's world you probably shouldn't. When I look at history, and I've studied the last 500 years of the rise and decline of empires and countries, I see the same cycle again and again. There's a debt cycle, an internal order and disorder cycle where the gap between the rich and the poor and the left and the right gets bigger, and an external cycle where great powers come into conflict. Those forces are acting on every country right now, so the question is really, where are those risks lowest and where are the strengths greatest?

So I'd look at a country the way I'd look at a company, by its fundamentals. Is it financially healthy? Does it earn more than it spends, or is it carrying a lot of debt it has to keep borrowing to service? Is there internal order? Do people get along well enough to be productive together, or is there a lot of polarization? Is there rule of law and civility, so the system works for you and not against you? Is the population well educated, and is there a culture of hard work and innovation? Then there's the external picture: is it likely to get caught in a war or a sanctions fight between great powers, or is it neutral enough that it can do business with all sides?

When you go through those indicators, a handful of places look good. Some smaller, well-run places like Singapore or some of the Gulf states have become hubs because they're stable, open, and neutral. India has a lot of things going for it. But no place is perfect, and that's the point. What I'd actually do is build the business so it's diversified. Put your legal structure in a place with strong rule of law. Keep your capital, your talent, and your customers in more than one jurisdiction, and make sure you can move if conditions change.

The biggest mistake people make is assuming the future will look like the recent past. The things that seemed impossible, like capital controls, asset seizures, or a country turning on itself, have happened many times in history. They just haven't happened in your lifetime. So build optionality in. Have a balanced portfolio of countries the same way you'd have a balanced portfolio of assets. That way you're not betting everything on one place being right.

r001.rationale: It discusses educated populations, innovation, and strong country fundamentals, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends diversifying the business across jurisdictions, including keeping capital, talent, and customers in more than one jurisdiction and maintaining a balanced portfolio of countries.

r003.rationale: It says conditions can change and advises building optionality so the business can move if they do, making clear that a location suitable now may not remain so over time.

fable-5.text:
Well, I think about it the same way I think about everything — which is to look at the cause-effect relationships and the measures that have, throughout history, determined which places rise and which places decline.

So if I were choosing where to build, I'd look at a few things. First, does the country earn more than it spends? Is it financially sound? Because countries with bad income statements and bad balance sheets eventually have debt problems, and debt problems lead to printing money, and printing money leads to currency devaluation and instability.

Second, I'd look at internal order. Is there civility? Do people respect the rule of law, or are they fighting with each other? Because when the gaps — wealth gaps, values gaps — get large and there's a lot of internal conflict, the environment becomes threatening. You can't build well in a place where people want to tear the system down, or where, if you're successful, you become a target.

Third — is it a civil, well-educated population? Education, inventiveness, productivity. Are people productive? Do they innovate?

And then there's the question of external conflict — is the country at risk of being in a war?

Now, your question is really the important one — how do you not tie yourself to one place? And I'd say: you have to think of it like a diversified portfolio. The biggest mistake people make is assuming that the place that's great now will be great in twenty years. History shows that's rarely true. Every country goes through the big cycle — they rise, they get overextended, they decline. So I'd build in a way that's mobile — keep the business flexible, keep assets in different places, make sure you have the ability to move.

I'd ask myself a simple question: if things got bad here — if there was a debt crisis, or internal conflict, or my taxes and freedoms changed dramatically — could I operate somewhere else? If the answer is no, you've taken on a risk that history says will eventually hurt you. Diversification — of location, of currency, of markets — is the one thing I know that improves your return relative to your risk without costing you anything. That's as true for choosing where to build a business as it is for investing.

r001.rationale: It mentions education, inventiveness, productivity, and innovation, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends flexibility, assets in different places, and geographic diversification, but does not clearly recommend maintaining business bases in multiple locations.

r003.rationale: It says the place that is great now may not be great in twenty years and describes countries rising and declining over time.

opus-5.text:
The way I think about it is this: don't fall in love with a place, measure it. I treat countries like I'd treat companies, because essentially that's what they are. So I'd look at the income statement and the balance sheet first. Is the government earning more than it's spending? Is it a creditor or a debtor? Who holds its debt, and are those holders willing buyers or captive buyers? Because a country that has to sell a lot of bonds to people who don't want them is going to have to either raise rates, print money, or raise taxes, and all three of those eventually come out of your pocket as a business owner.

Then I'd look at internal order. How big is the wealth gap, how big is the values gap, and is there a rule of law that holds regardless of who's in power? What I care about isn't whether I like the politics. What I care about is predictability — can I know what the rules will be in ten years? And you can see that in the behavior. When people start fighting rather than following agreed-upon procedures to resolve disputes, that's the signal, and it's usually visible well before the crisis.

Third, external order. Is it in the middle of a geopolitical fault line? Who are its allies, and if a conflict happens, which side does it have to pick?

And then the practical things: quality of people, education, work ethic, infrastructure, taxes, whether capital can get in and out freely.

But here's the part that answers your question most directly. You don't solve this by picking the right country. You solve it by not needing to be right. I'd be in at least a few places that are not correlated with each other — different currencies, different legal systems, different geopolitical sponsors. I'd hold assets in more than one jurisdiction. I'd build the business so that the loss of any single location is survivable rather than fatal. People think diversification is for portfolios. It's just as true for where you put your life and your operations.

The mistake I see most often is that people assume the place that's been good to them will continue to be good to them. That's an extrapolation, and it works right up until it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response mentions people, education, and work ethic as factors, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends being in “at least a few places” and holding assets in more than one jurisdiction, with operations resilient to losing any single location.

r003.rationale: It says a place that has been good may not continue to be good and calls assuming otherwise an extrapolation.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd start from the fact that the world has changed. For a long time you could think of one country as your home and your market, but the big shifts now are the rise of China, the relative decline of the West in some areas, rising internal conflict within countries, and a more fragmented world order. So I wouldn't ask "which country is best?" I'd ask "how do I avoid being dependent on any single one?"

I'd look at a few things. First is the strength of a country's fundamentals: education, innovation, competitiveness, productivity, and whether it has strong capital markets and the rule of law. Those are the things that make a place a good base for building something. Second is the health of its finances and its politics. A country with heavy debt, big wealth gaps, and severe political polarization is more likely to see sudden changes in taxes, in rules, or in what you're allowed to do with your money. I'd call that the risk of a regime change, and I would not want my entire business exposed to it.

Then I'd separate where I'm based from where I operate. You can have your home base where the legal system and talent are strong, but you serve customers in many markets, hire talent from many places, and hold your assets in different currencies and jurisdictions. It's the same principle as in investing. I'd rather have a number of good, uncorrelated bets than one great bet, because I know I can't predict the future with certainty. Diversification is the closest thing to a free lunch.

I'd also stay flexible. Conditions change, so I'd want the freedom to move capital, people, or operations if the environment shifts. I'd look for places that are open to outsiders, and I'd study how the cycles are moving in each place before I commit.

r001.rationale: It mentions innovation and talent as factors, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends serving multiple markets and hiring across places, but describes a single home base and does not recommend maintaining business bases in multiple geographic locations.

r003.rationale: It says conditions change and recommends staying flexible enough to move capital, people, or operations when the environment shifts, conveying that a location’s suitability can change over time.

haiku-5.5.text:
The first thing I'd look at is rule of law and whether your contracts and property will hold up over decades. A country can have a great market today and still change the rules on you, through taxes, capital controls, or simply a government that stops respecting what was agreed. So I'd ask where you can own things, enforce agreements, and move money out if you need to.

Then I'd think about diversification the way I think about investments. You don't want all your bets moving together. If your customers, your team, your banking, and your legal entity all sit in one place, one bad political or economic cycle can hit all of them at once. Spreading those pieces across places that aren't highly correlated gives you real resilience.

I'd also pay attention to where the talent is and where the customers are growing, not just where costs are lowest. And I'd be careful about the trade-off between flexibility and complexity. Multiple jurisdictions bring tax and compliance work, so you need a good advisor and a clear structure from the start.

Finally, I'd set up the business so it could operate from several places if necessary. Then you're choosing a home, not depending on one.

r001.rationale: It mentions considering where talent is, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It recommends spreading business components across places and being able to operate from several places if needed, but does not clearly recommend maintaining business bases in multiple locations.

r003.rationale: It says a country with a great market today may change its rules over time, making clear that a location’s current advantages may not last.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it as a diversification decision. Where you live, where you establish the business, where you hire people, and where your customers are don’t necessarily have to be the same place.

Then I’d ask: What does this business need to succeed? Where is the talent? Are the laws clear and dependable? Can I move capital? Is it a place where I’d want my family and my employees to live? Taxes are part of that calculation, but they’re only one part.

And then you have to ask, what happens if I’m wrong? If conditions in that country change, can the business still function? Can I move? Do I have customers and resources elsewhere?

You need enough of a base to build something well, while preserving the ability to adapt. I’d want my success to depend on serving customers well, with as little dependence as practical on any single country’s future.

r001.rationale: It asks where the talent is, but does not recommend locating near concentrations of people doing cutting-edge work.

r002.rationale: It mentions customers and resources elsewhere and the ability to move, but does not clearly recommend maintaining business bases in multiple locations.

r003.rationale: It notes that conditions in a country can change and asks whether the business could still function, conveying that a location’s suitability may change over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d approach it the way I’d approach a portfolio. I’d look globally for the best combination of talent, customers, opportunity, and a legal system I can depend on. And I’d think carefully about how much of my future depends on that one place.

You can have a main base and still build an international business. Your customers can be in different countries, your team can be in different locations, and you can preserve the ability to change where you operate. There’s a cost to that complexity, so it has to serve the business.

The important thing is to have options. Countries change, policies change, opportunities change. I’d choose a place where the business can thrive today, while building enough flexibility to adapt if the circumstances change.

You don’t have to be everywhere. You want a strong base and the flexibility to adapt as conditions change.

terra-5.6.text:
I’d think of it first as a question of diversification. You don’t want your fate to be entirely tied to one country’s politics, taxes, currency, or economic cycle. So I’d ask: where are the people, the markets, the talent, and the rule of law that my business needs—and then build the company so it can operate across several jurisdictions.

The key is to have a home base without having a single point of failure. Be clear about where decisions are made, where intellectual property sits, where customers are, and where capital can move. Then design for resilience: multiple suppliers, multiple banking relationships, and teams in different places. The world changes, and you want to be able to adapt rather than be trapped by a change in one country.

Then I’d avoid making any one country a single point of failure. You can build a global structure—teams, suppliers, banking relationships, and legal entities across several jurisdictions—while keeping a strong culture and clear decision-making at the center. The key is to think in terms of diversification: understand each country’s rules, political risks, taxes, and strengths, and design the business so it can adapt if conditions change.
